blocks.md:
- During a reaction, the **reactants** are used up and changed into the **products**
- This means that as the reaction proceeds, the concentration of reactants **decreases **and the concentration of products **increases**
- Therefore, the **rate of the reaction** is not the same throughout the reaction but **changes**
- The rate of reaction during the reaction can be calculated from a **concentration-time graph.**
- The **isomerisation of cyclopropane** to propene will be taken as an example:

blocks.alt: Chemical reaction: Cyclopropane gas to propene gas, showing molecular structures. Cyclopropane as reactant, propene as product.
blocks.caption: The reactant cyclopropane isomerises to form propene

blocks.md: - The concentrations of reactant (cyclopropane) and product (propene) over time can be experimentally obtained

blocks.text: Concentrations of cyclopropane & propene results table

blocks.md:
- When taking the measurements, the **temperature** should be kept the same at all times as a **change** in temperature will change the **rate of reaction**
- A **concentration-time graph** for the **concentration of propene as well as cyclopropane** can be obtained from the above results

  - As an example, the concentration-time graph for propene is shown below:

blocks.alt: Graph showing propene concentration in mol/dm³ against time in minutes. Purple curve rises, with red lines and crosses indicating data points.
blocks.caption: The graph shows that the concentration of propene increases with time

blocks.text: Calculating the rate at the start of a reaction

blocks.md:
- At the start of the reaction, the concentration-time curve looks almost linear
- The rate at this point can therefore be found by treating the curve as a linear line and by using:
- Using the graph, the average rate of the reaction over the first 5 minutes for propene is:

blocks.alt: Graph showing propene concentration over time. Black and red lines with labels a and b; dashed lines mark 0.3 mol dm⁻³ at 5 minutes.
blocks.caption: Line (a) shows the average rate over the first five minutes whereas line (b) shows the actual initial rate found by drawing a tangent at the start of the curve. The calculated rates are very similar for both methods.

blocks.md:
- Rate of reaction = $\frac{\mathrm{change} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{amount} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{reactants} \mathrm{or} \mathrm{products}(\mathrm{mol} \mathrm{dm}^{-3})}{\mathrm{time}(s)}$

  - Rate of reaction =$\frac{0.27}{300}$
  - Rate of reaction = 0.0009 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>

blocks.text: Calculating the rate as the reaction proceeds

blocks.md:
- The curve becomes shallower with time which means that the rate decreases with time
- The rate of reaction can be calculated by taking short time intervals

  - For example, the rate of reaction from 15 to 20 mins
  - During this time, the concentration of propene increases from 0.68 to 0.83 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>:

- Rate of reaction = $\frac{\mathrm{change} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{amount} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{reactants} \mathrm{or} \mathrm{products}(\mathrm{mol} \mathrm{dm}^{-3})}{\mathrm{time}(s)}$

  - Rate of reaction =$\frac{( 0.83 ) - ( 0.68 )}{( 1200 ) - ( 900 )}$
  - Rate of reaction = $\frac{0.14}{300}$
  - Rate of reaction = 0.0005 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>

- The smaller the time intervals, the more accurate the reaction rate value is
- Even more accurate is to find the rate of reaction at **different concentrations **of reactant or product at **particular time** **points**
- This can be done by drawing **tangents **at several points on the graph

  - As an example, the rates of reaction at different concentrations of cyclopropane are calculated by drawing the appropriate tangents:

blocks.text: Calculating rate as a reaction progresses

blocks.alt: Graph showing concentration of cyclopropane over time with tangents and labelled points. Rates at concentrations 1.5, 1.0, and 0.5 mol dm⁻³ are calculated.
blocks.caption: The rate of reaction at 3 different concentrations of cyclopropane is calculated by drawing tangents at those points in the graph

blocks.md: - The calculated rates can then be summarised in a table to show how the rate of reaction changes with changing concentration of the reactants or products

blocks.text: Change in rate with decreasing concentration of cyclopropane table

blocks.md:
- This data can then be used to plot a rate-concentration graph
- The graph shows that the rate is directly proportional to the concentration of cyclopropane

  - If you double the concentration of cyclopropane the rate of reaction will double too

blocks.alt: Graph of cyclopropane rate of decrease against concentration, with a linear trendline and three red asterisks on dashed red lines at three data points.
blocks.caption: The graph shows a directly proportional correlation between the concentration of cyclopropane and the rate of reaction

blocks.label: Exam Hint
blocks.md: To calculate the rate of reaction you can either use the increase in concentration of products (like in the example above) or the decrease in concentration of reactants.
